implementation_notes: Rust's compiler enforces a great deal, so its mud is a single crate with wide module coupling rather than a dependency cycle — every module is compiled together and every `pub use` from `lib.rs` widens the surface. The rustc module graph plus `cargo`'s crate graph are both mechanically inspectable, and moving a module into its own crate is a compiler-checked refactoring. The mud-specific hazard is a `prelude`/`mod.rs` that re-exports everything, which reproduces the barrel problem from JavaScript in a language where it could have been prevented.
idiom_name: one crate with every module re-exported from lib.rs
pitfalls: `pub use x::*` re-exports everything the module has, so one line in `lib.rs` silently republishes an entire subsystem's API.
Feature flags can make a dependency graph differ per build configuration, so the graph you measure is not the graph production runs.
`pub(crate)` is the right default; anything wider is mud surface that the compiler will not question.
